q-161311.name: Question 1
q-161311.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14226282/assets/5ba2dbc746b9fe8b36202d31bbeb8193ffb9e747d6ed4c2e2f0f994499f88e8e.png)

Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}S,
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=-x+\sqrt{2}y$ and whose domain is the quarter-circle of radius $3$ centered at $O$ in the second quadrant, as shown above.
q-161311.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(-x+\sqrt{2}y)=-1,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(-x+\sqrt{2}y)=\sqrt{2}.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{1+(-1)^{2}+(\sqrt{2})^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{4}\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{∬}_{D}\,\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ our domain can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi \}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}2{∬}_{D}\,\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & =2{∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta  \\  & =2{∬}_{Δ}\frac{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\cdot r\text{ }\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{∬}_{Δ}\frac{{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{∬}_{Δ}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}r \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{3}{[\,\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\,]}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\,\text{d}r \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{3}(-1)\,\text{d}r \\  & =2\cdot (-1)\cdot 3 \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

q-161311.html:
Question 1
?

Evaluate the surface integral ∬Sxx2+y2dS, where S is defined by z=−x+2y and whose domain is the quarter-circle of radius 3 centered at O in the second quadrant, as shown above.

a
16
b
2
c
−6
d
13
e
3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a surface S defined by z=g(x,y) with (x,y)∈D, the surface integral of a scalar function f(x,y,z) over S is given by

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬Df(x,y,g(x,y))1+(∂z∂x)2+(∂z∂y)2dA.

For the partial derivatives, we have

∂z∂x=∂∂x(−x+2y)=−1, and ∂z∂y=∂∂y(−x+2y)=2.

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

∬Sxx2+y2dS=∬Df(x,y,g(x,y))1+(∂z∂x)2+(∂z∂y)2dA=∬Dxx2+y2⋅1+(−1)2+(2)2dA=∬Dxx2+y2⋅4dA=2∬Dxx2+y2dA.

Notice that in polar coordinates (r,θ), our domain can be expressed as

Δ={(r,θ):0≤r≤3,π2≤θ≤π}.

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where x=rcos⁡θ and y=rsin⁡θ, we obtain

2∬Dxx2+y2dA=2∬Δ f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r drdθ=2∬Δrcos⁡θr2cos2⁡θ+r2sin2⁡θ⋅r drdθ=2∬Δr2cos⁡θr2(cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ)drdθ=2∬Δcos⁡θdrdθ=2∫03∫π/2πcos⁡θdθdr=2∫03[sin⁡θ]π/2πdr=2∫03(−1)dr=2⋅(−1)⋅3=−6.

q-161339.name: Question 2
q-161339.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14226282/assets/d19d54d0e76ced24d1bd9f865578b72f2b8d67414c8506499c6ae7b1300a6275.png)

Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}(x+y)\,\text{d}S,
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=-2x+2y$ and whose domain is the left half-circle of radius $1$ centered at $O$, as shown above.
q-161339.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(-2x+2y)=-2,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(-2x+2y)=2.
$$

 

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}(x+y)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(x+y)\cdot \sqrt{1+(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(x+y)\cdot \sqrt{9}\,\text{d}A \\  & =3{∬}_{D}\,(x+y)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ our domain can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2}\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}3{∬}_{D}\,(x+y)\,\text{d}A & =3{∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta  \\  & =3{∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\cdot r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{∬}_{Δ}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ){\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ){[\frac{{r}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =[\,\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the surface integral ∬S(x+y)dS, where S is defined by z=−2x+2y and whose domain is the left half-circle of radius 1 centered at O, as shown above.

a
5
b
4
c
−1
d
−2
e
8

Incorrect
EXPLANATION

For a surface S defined by z=g(x,y) with (x,y)∈D, the surface integral of a scalar function f(x,y,z) over S is given by

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬Df(x,y,g(x,y))1+(∂z∂x)2+(∂z∂y)2dA.

For the partial derivatives, we have

∂z∂x=∂∂x(−2x+2y)=−2, and ∂z∂y=∂∂y(−2x+2y)=2.

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

∬S(x+y)dS=∬Df(x,y,g(x,y))1+(∂z∂x)2+(∂z∂y)2dA=∬D(x+y)⋅1+(−2)2+22dA=∬D(x+y)⋅9dA=3∬D(x+y)dA.

Notice that in polar coordinates (r,θ), our domain can be expressed as

Δ={(r,θ):0≤r≤1,π2≤θ≤3π2}.

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where x=rcos⁡θ and y=rsin⁡θ, we obtain

3∬D(x+y)dA=3∬Δ f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r drdθ=3∬Δ(rcos⁡θ+rsin⁡θ)⋅rdrdθ=3∬Δr2(cos⁡θ+sin⁡θ)drdθ=3∫π/23π/2(cos⁡θ+sin⁡θ)∫01r2drdθ=3∫π/23π/2(cos⁡θ+sin⁡θ)[r33]01dθ=∫π/23π/2(cos⁡θ+sin⁡θ)dθ=[sin⁡θ−cos⁡θ]π/23π/2=−2.

q-161341.name: Question 3
q-161341.problem:
Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}4z\,\text{d}S
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=x+y$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$
q-161341.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+y)=1,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y)=1.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be evaluated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}4z\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,4(x+y)\,\sqrt{1+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}4(x+y)\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}{[4xy+2{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}(4x+2)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{3}{[2{x}^{2}+2x]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =4\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

q-161351.name: Question 4
q-161351.problem:
Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}(24xy+{z}^{2})\,\text{d}S
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=3x-4y$ for $1\le x\le 2$ and $0\le y\le 1.$
q-161351.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(3x-4y)=3,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(3x-4y)=-4.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be evaluated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}(24xy+{z}^{2})\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,(24xy+(3x-4y)^{2})\sqrt{1+{3}^{2}+(-4)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{26}{∬}_{D}\,(24xy+9{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}-24xy)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{26}{∬}_{D}\,(9{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{26}{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(9{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{26}{\int }_{1}^{2}{[9{x}^{2}y+\frac{16}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{26}{\int }_{1}^{2}(9{x}^{2}+\frac{16}{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{26}{[3{x}^{3}+\frac{16}{3}x]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =\sqrt{26}(24+\frac{32}{3}-3-\frac{16}{3}) \\  & =\frac{79}{3}\sqrt{26}\end{aligned}
$$

q-161355.name: Question 5
q-161355.problem:
Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}\frac{z}{\sqrt{1+2{cos}^{2}⁡(x+y)}}\,\text{d}S
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)$ for $0\le x\le \pi $ and $-x\le y\le x.$
q-161355.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y),
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y).
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be evaluated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\frac{z}{\sqrt{1+2{cos}^{2}⁡(x+y)}}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)}{\sqrt{1+2{cos}^{2}⁡(x+y)}}\sqrt{1+2(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y))^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)}{\cancel{\sqrt{1+2{cos}^{2}⁡(x+y)}}}\cancel{\sqrt{1+2(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y))^{2}}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{-x}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)]_{y=-x}^{y=x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x))\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[x-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}]}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\pi \end{aligned}
$$
